Article Title: A Delaware father left an IRA worth about $438,000 with instructions for his four children; the custodian omitted crucial words, triggering a $55,000-per-child dispute that a November 12 court settled
Article Text:

What Harkins intended

What Fidelity recorded

The two interpretations

How the court decided

What this decision means

What happens next

William F. Harkins wanted his four children to receive equal shares of an individual retirement account worth about $438,000 when he died in February 2025. He directed 25 percent each to two children and left the remaining 50 percent to his revocable trust for the benefit of special needs trusts created for his other two children, but Fidelity’s records omitted the crucial “for the benefit of” language, triggering a family dispute over roughly $55,000 per child, according to the Delaware Court of Chancery’s November 12 decision on Justia U.S. Law.The court found that Harkins substantially complied with the requirements for changing the beneficiary designation, even though the custodian did not fully record his instructions. That finding means the 50 percent share must go to the special needs trusts for Marie and Ruth, rather than being divided equally among all four children. Read more about this case, as per the record, here:Harkins and his wife, Marie, created a revocable joint trust in 2013, later restated in 2019. The trust divided assets into four equal shares for their four adult children, with Marie and Ruth’s shares held in special needs trusts because they could not receive funds directly.After Marie’s death in January 2023, Harkins submitted a beneficiary designation form to Fidelity in May 2023. He designated 25 percent each to Kim and Tom, and directed the remaining 50 percent to an “Other Entity,” with instructions to see an attached letter.That letter clearly stated that the third beneficiary should be the “Revocable Trust of William F. Harkins and Marie V. Harkins, U/A 12/3/2013, as amended, Article 8-B Trusts f/b/o Ruth Anne Harkins and Marie J. Harkins.” It also directed that the funds be held, administered, and distributed according to the trust’s terms.Fidelity’s records initially identified the third beneficiary as “Rev Tru Of William Marie Harkins U/A 12/[sic],” which did not include the “for the benefit of” language or the reference to the special needs trusts. After the error was brought to its attention, Fidelity corrected the name to “Revocable Trust of William F. Harkins and Marie V. Harkins” but still did not include the additional language from Harkins’s letter.Fidelity distributed 25 percent of the IRA outright to Kim and 25 percent to Tom, consistent with the beneficiary designation form. The remaining 50 percent was held in an inherited IRA in the name of the revocable trust.That omission created the dispute. If the 50 percent share were divided equally among all four children, Kim and Tom would each end up with 37.5 percent of the total IRA, while Marie and Ruth would each receive 12.5 percent.Three of the children, Kim, Marie, and Ruth, argued that the “for the benefit of” language should be honored, meaning the 50 percent share should go to the special needs trusts for Marie and Ruth. That would give each of the four children 25 percent of the total IRA.Tom and his daughter Jaclyn argued that the custodian’s omission should be honored, meaning the 50 percent share should be divided equally among all four children. Their position would give Kim and Tom 37.5 percent each and Marie and Ruth 12.5 percent each.The difference amounts to about $55,000 per child, based on the February 2025 value of the IRA. That is a significant amount, and it explains why the family could not simply agree to move on.The court applied Delaware’s doctrine of substantial compliance, which allows a court to give effect to an intended change in beneficiary even if formal requirements were not strictly met. To establish substantial compliance, the proponent must show that the account owner intended the change and did all that was reasonably possible to effect it.The court found that Harkins’s form and attached letter clearly showed his intent to direct the 50 percent share to the special needs trusts. He completed the form, signed and dated it, and explicitly instructed Fidelity to consult the attached letter.The court also noted that it may have been impossible to fit all of the letter’s language into the limited space on Fidelity’s form. That practical reality buttressed the conclusion that Harkins did everything reasonably possible to make his intent clear.The ruling makes it clear that a custodian's failure to fully document instructions doesn't necessarily defeat the account owner's intent. If the owner took clear, affirmative steps to direct the funds, the court can still honor that intent.The case serves as a reminder to families about the importance of specificity in naming beneficiaries, particularly in the setting of trusts and special needs planning.A missing phrase can lead to a dispute costing tens of thousands of dollars and taking years to resolve.It also stresses the need to include a brief letter of instruction if there is insufficient space on the form. In this case, that letter was the key evidence that allowed the court to determine what Harkins actually wanted.The court granted summary judgment in favor of Kim, the petitioner. That means the 50 percent share of the IRA must be distributed to the special needs trusts for Marie and Ruth, not divided equally among all four children.Any party seeking to challenge the decision had until November 23, 2026, to file exceptions. The ruling is a final report under Court of Chancery Rule 144(b)(2), which means it carries significant weight unless successfully challenged.For the Harkins family, the court’s decision brings clarity to a painful and expensive dispute. It also illustrates how good estate planning—and a clear paper trail—can make the difference between a smooth transition and an expensive legal battle.
Article Summary: William F. Harkins wanted his four children to receive equal shares of an individual retirement account worth about $438,000 when he died in February 2025. He directed 25 percent each to two children and left the remaining 50 percent to his revocable trust. Fidelity’s records omitted the crucial “for the benefit of” language, triggering a family dispute over roughly $55,000 per child.

Article Title: Cape Verde president Jose Maria Neves re-elected with 64% of votes, defeats first-ever woman candidate
Article Text:
File photo: Supporters celebrate with Cape Verde’s President Jose Maria Neves after his victory in the presidential election in Praia, Cape Verde

Low turnout raises questions

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cape Verde president José Maria Neves has won a second five-year term, securing 64% of the vote and defeating five challengers, including the country's first woman presidential candidate, Joana Rosa, according to provisional results.Rosa, the main opposition candidate, received 31.4% of the vote and called Neves to concede defeat. Neves described his victory as “a great victory” in a speech after the results were announced.The election was held against a backdrop of high unemployment, rising living costs and sustained emigration, with many young Cape Verdeans leaving the Atlantic island nation in search of opportunities abroad.“The president of the republic does not have a majority; the president of the republic belongs to everyone,” Neves said, seeking to underline the largely non-partisan nature of the office.Turnout was low, with only 31.7% of the 418,000 registered voters casting their ballots. Neves attributed the poor participation to high emigration, population movements within the country and outdated voter records. He promised a study to examine the reasons behind the low turnout.The election had drawn attention because Rosa was the first woman to contest the presidency since the country gained independence in 1975.However, the result gives Neves a second consecutive term, extending his tenure as head of state.Cape Verde is regarded as one of West Africa's more politically stable countries, with a record of peaceful transfers of power in a region that has experienced coups and disputed elections.Under its parliamentary system, the prime minister holds most executive authority and directs government policy. The president is directly elected but has a largely ceremonial role, with powers that include vetoing legislation.
Article Summary: Cape Verde president Jose Maria Neves has won a second five-year term. He secured 64% of the vote and defeated five challengers, including the country's first woman presidential candidate, Joana Rosa. Neves described his victory as ‘a great victory’

NBA legend Ben Wallace is preparing to part ways with his sprawling Goochland County mansion. The 35-acre property is on the market with an asking price of $6.9 million, according to Athlon Sports.Former Detroit Pistons star Ben Wallace and his wife, Chanda, bought the land for $790,000 before construction began. The couple wanted a private retreat close to the Richmond area, where Wallace’s basketball journey began. The estate spans more than 22,308 sq. ft. across 35 acres divided into three parcels. The European-style home, located at 785 Oak Spring Lane in the Manakin-Sabot area, was completed in 2015.The house has six bedrooms, six full bathrooms and seven half-bathrooms. A two-storey foyer opens onto curved staircases and a floating catwalk, setting the tone for the rest of the property. “The living room features soaring ceilings, walls of windows, and refined architectural details. Travertine and cherry hardwood floors, detailed millwork, and custom mouldings showcase craftsmanship throughout,” the listing on Redfin describes.The primary suite is a “private haven”, the listing says. It features a lounge with a curved wall of windows, a drop-down TV, and dry and wet bars. The spa-style en suite features a large steam shower, jacuzzi tub, and double vanities. The primary suite also has two closets, including a two-storey designer space with granite counters, built-ins, a wine dispenser, and seating.The house also comes with a chef’s kitchen equipped with Wolf, Sub-Zero, and Asko appliances. According to the listing, the lower level is designed entirely for entertaining, with a game room, full bar, weight room, and indoor sports court featuring a climbing wall and viewing balcony. It is a fitting addition for a former NBA defensive standout. A full elevator, mudroom, and double laundry rooms take care of everyday needs.Outside, the property has a Gunite infinity-edge pool, a hot tub, and a screened porch overlooking the pool, pond, and woods. The property is also ideal for a motorhead. The house has a six-car attached garage and a detached garage that can accommodate seven or more vehicles. The listing also mentions geothermal heating and cooling, a whole-house generator, and pond-fed irrigation. “A true masterpiece, retreat, and legacy — this is the one with every possibility,” the listing says.Wallace has listed the property with Sharon Ligon of Sotheby’s International Realty. The property is already attracting interest from local and out-of-town buyers, according to Ligon. One of its biggest selling points is the range of possibilities it offers.“It could be multigenerational, it could just be a single-family, it could be an investor. Who knows? It’s just a very special property. People need to see it to appreciate it, because it’s just unique for the area,” she told Richmond BizSense.The $6.9 million asking price is below Goochland County’s assessment, which exceeds $8 million. Ligon agrees: “It’s 35 acres, a large, large house, and you could not build that house for the price that we came up with. The reason was simply because everybody’s going to want a perfect house, and there’s not the perfect house.”Meanwhile, Wallace has also sold Big Ben’s Home Court, his indoor basketball facility in Henrico. The estate’s listing entered the regional multiple listing service about three months after that sale. The two moves suggest a shift in how Wallace is managing his Virginia real estate holdings.
Article Summary: Former Detroit Pistons star Ben Wallace and his wife, Chanda, bought the land for $790,000 before construction began. The European-style home, located at 785 Oak Spring Lane in the Manakin-Sabot area, was completed in 2015. The house has six bedrooms, six full bathrooms and seven half-bathrooms.

Article Title: Former firefighter Martin Hunt, 27, left Goldman Sachs to build Garage, an online marketplace for used fire trucks; it now handles $100 million a year in sales and has just been valued at $225 million
Article Text:

The fire engine that once carried Martin Hunt to his first emergency call was expected to fetch just $30,000 when his hometown fire department decided to sell it. Instead, the ageing vehicle found a buyer within days for $125,000 through an online marketplace Hunt himself had helped build. The sale offered a striking demonstration of the problem he had set out to solve: equipment that one community no longer needed could still be worth a great deal to another. As Fortune reported on November 10, Hunt, now 27, has turned that insight into Garage, a used-equipment marketplace valued at $225 million after its latest funding round.Hunt's journey to entrepreneurship began long before his career in finance. At 15, he joined the volunteer fire service in northern Delaware, near Philadelphia. Alongside responding to emergencies, he gradually took on responsibilities that were less visible but essential to keeping the department operational, including helping sell older fire trucks when they were replaced.The process was far from straightforward. Fire departments often need to sell ageing engines to recover some of the money spent on new equipment.But finding buyers could involve calling departments across the country, relying on word of mouth or sending vehicles to local auctions. A truck that remained perfectly usable could end up selling for a fraction of its potential value, or even being treated as scrap.The challenge stayed with Hunt even after he moved into the world of finance. By 2023, he was working as a private equity investor at Goldman Sachs. Then a former colleague from his fire department contacted him for advice on selling equipment. The conversation brought back a familiar frustration: despite the passage of years, departments were still relying on largely manual methods to buy and sell specialised vehicles.Hunt began exploring whether the process could be moved online. He joined forces with Alaz Sengul, whom he had met through a mutual friend at Columbia University. Sengul brought software experience from companies including Twitter, now known as X, and artificial intelligence startup Mem. Hunt, meanwhile, understood the needs of the departments they hoped to serve. The two decided to leave their jobs and build the business without an existing product or outside funding, relying on their savings as they worked on the idea. They joined Y Combinator's winter 2024 programme, moved to San Francisco and launched Garage early that year.The platform is designed to connect fire departments and other organisations looking to sell surplus equipment with buyers searching for affordable alternatives to new vehicles. It does not purchase or store the trucks itself. Instead, vehicles remain with their owners until a sale is completed, after which they are transported to their new locations.The distinction matters in a market where equipment is expensive, specialised and difficult to move. A new fire engine can cost millions of dollars and take years to arrive, while a used vehicle can offer a faster and more affordable option for a department working with limited public funds. Garage's November funding announcement said communities could acquire a high-quality used fire truck for around $150,000, compared with as much as $2 million for a new one.Garage attempts to simplify the transaction through artificial intelligence-based appraisals, freight coordination and delivery estimates. It also offers financing and optional warranties. According to Hunt, more than 90 per cent of transactions cross state lines, with equipment travelling an average of 1,400 miles. A buyer in one part of the country can therefore find a vehicle being sold by a department hundreds or thousands of miles away.The company says it now serves more than 1,000 communities across all 50 US states and Canada. Equipment sales through the platform have crossed $100 million on an annualised basis, while its November 10 announcement reported growth of more than 400 per cent year on year. The $100 million figure represents the value of transactions facilitated through the marketplace, not Garage's own revenue, which has not been disclosed. Fortune reported that the company charges sellers a 10 per cent success fee on buy-now purchases and buyers a 10 per cent premium at auction.The latest milestone came with a $41 million Series B funding round led by Invus Opportunities. The investment values Garage at $225 million and takes its total funding to $60 million. Other investors named in the company's announcement include Infinity Ventures, Initialized Capital, Y Combinator, Benchstrength and FJ Labs.For some communities, the marketplace's impact can be measured in money recovered from equipment that might otherwise have fetched much less. South Charleston, West Virginia, had expected to bring in a few hundred thousand dollars from surplus equipment sales in 2025, but generated $1.2 million through Garage, Hunt told Fortune. The proceeds helped fund replacement equipment and cancer screenings for firefighters. In another example cited by the company, a fire department in Burlington, Vermont, reported receiving about five times more for its equipment than it had through its earlier selling methods.Hunt and Sengul are now looking beyond emergency vehicles. The latest funding is intended to support hiring and expansion into categories such as public works and sanitation equipment. Private sanitation companies are already among Garage's fastest-growing customer groups, Hunt told Fortune.The ambition is substantial, but Hunt believes the company has only begun tapping the market. Even in used fire trucks, where Garage describes itself as the country's largest source, he estimates it currently serves about 1 per cent of the market.For someone who once spent his time helping a local fire department find buyers for old engines, the business has grown far beyond its original setting. Its central idea, however, remains rooted in that early experience, a vehicle that has reached the end of its service in one town may still have years of work ahead of it somewhere else.
Article Summary: Garage is a used-equipment marketplace valued at $225 million. It connects fire departments and other organisations looking to sell surplus equipment with buyers searching for affordable alternatives to new vehicles. The company says it now serves more than 1,000 communities across all 50 states and Canada.

Article Title: At 15, Abuja student Khaira Ojima Bala won Nigeria's national essay competition from more than 15,000 entries and received a ₦15 million university grant; her winning essay tackled the country's food-
Article Text:
Bala triumphed over 15,000 entries, winning the national competition on her first attempt through dedication.

Student in Abuja bags top honors from thousands

Food security becomes center stage

UBA increases educational grants to N41 million

A 16-year investment in young players

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Many teenagers are still trying to figure out what they want to do with their lives, but 15-year-old Khaira Ojima Bala has already won national recognition for her writing and understanding of critical development issues. The Abuja-based student has emerged winner of the 2026 UBA Foundation National Essay Competition, beating thousands of secondary school students across Nigeria to clinch a ₦15million educational grant. Her achievement underscores the growing importance of cultivating young intellectual potential and encouraging students to engage in the contests that will shape the nation’s destiny.According to a report by the Daily Trust, Bala, a student of Metro International School in Abuja emerged the overall winner at the competition’s grand finale and award presentation ceremony held at UBA House, Marina, Lagos.More than 15,000 entries were received from senior secondary school students across the country for the 16th edition of the annual competition, the report states. And the Nigerian Tribune reports that the SS3 science student achieved the feat on her first attempt after putting in a lot of hard work to prepare her entry.For the first place, she won ₦15 million educational grant to continue her university education at any university of her choice across Africa, a trophy, laptop and certificate of merit.Generous educational grants also went to other top contenders in the competition. Unwanabasi Otobong Udom of Topfaith International Secondary School, Akwa Ibom came second with ₦10 million. Flourish Chibunumona Ndamzi of University of Port Harcourt Women Association International Secondary School got third place with ₦7.5 million, the online report states.Godsfavour Ezekiel Udo of Federal Government Girls College, Ikot Obio Itong, came fourth and won ₦5 million, while Uchenna Olivia Anyanwu of Coral Impacts International School, Abuja, came fifth and won ₦3.5 million.The competition encouraged participants to research, analyze and put forward written arguments on some of Nigeria’s pressing development challenges.This year’s essay topic, according to Daily Trust, was on the relationship between national development and food security, and students were tasked to explore how Nigeria can tackle the challenge, the Daily Trust report adds.The judges then chose the 20 finalists from the entries submitted from all over the country. The finalists were then invited to a one day writing boot camp run by the judges. The program was an opportunity to refine their writing skills and prepare them for the final stretch.Female students dominated the competition, taking all the top five places and seven of the other 20 finalists, The Nigerian Tribune report said.This year there was also a substantial hike in the financial support for the competitors. The Daily Trust reports that total allocation for educational grant increased to ₦41million, an 82% increase from ₦22.5million released in 2025. With the expansion, the foundation was able to offer scholarship grants to five winners instead of three, with the fourth- and fifth-place participants receiving university grants for the first time in the competition’s history.All the 20 finalists also received laptops to aid their education and research and ₦20,000 each was credited into their UBA accounts.Oliver Alawuba, the Group Managing Director of UBA, said the improved rewards were in recognition of the rising cost of university education and the financial challenges families were facing due to inflation. He also emphasized the significance of preparing the young people of Africa to participate in the development of the continent.In 2011, the UBA Foundation, the corporate social responsibility arm of United Bank for Africa, initiated the National Essay Competition in Nigeria. The initiative has spread over the years to other African countries where the Bank operates.The foundation has invested over N3 billion in the competition in its 16 editions, Daily Trust quoted its Managing Director, Bola Atta, as saying.The initiative has also helped to improve the writing skills, confidence, critical thinking and consciousness of national issues of the students, the Nigerian Tribune further reported.The judges also stressed the need for students to do more research and independent thinking, expressing concern that some students submitted work that wasn’t well-aligned with the topics of the essays or relied too much on artificial intelligence tools.The N15 million grant for Bala is more than a win in a competition. It offers her the chance to pursue higher education and place her among a new generation of Nigerian students who are being recognized for their intellectual contributions. Her achievement also signals the power of education initiatives to inspire young people to tackle the country’s most pressing challenges.Image Courtesy: Facebook
Article Summary: Khaira Ojima Bala, 15, won the 2026 UBA Foundation National Essay Competition on her first attempt. The science student from Abuja beat thousands of secondary school students across Nigeria to clinch a ₦15million educational grant. The competition encouraged participants to research, analyze and put forward written arguments on some of Nigeria’s pressing development challenges.

Article Title: Ukraine launches biggest drone attack on Russia; Moscow says over 1,300 drones intercepted
Article Text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Russia said its air defence systems intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones on Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv’s largest aerial assault since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.According to the Associated Press (AP), Ukraine has stepped up its long-range drone attacks on Russian territory, as well as Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, with some recent operations involving more than 1,000 drones.Moscow, meanwhile, has continued its attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, particularly the power grid, in strikes that Kyiv says are aimed at disrupting everyday life and weakening public morale.Ukraine's strikes on Russian territory have increasingly focused on oil refineries, a key source of revenue for Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Sunday that attacks by his forces had knocked out more than 55% of Russia's oil refining capacity.Russian authorities have not responded to Zelenskyy's claim, and it could not be independently verified.Kyiv is also seeking to bring the impact of the war closer to ordinary Russians.Ukrainian mid-range drone strikes have disrupted Russian supply routes to the front lines and complicated Moscow's military operations, analysts say.Ukraine has also blamed recently imposed speed restrictions on the US-made Starshield satellite system for weakening its air defence capabilities. Starshield, developed by SpaceX, is the military-grade version of its Starlink satellite internet service.Ukrainian forces say they are targeting Russian weapons manufacturing facilities and locations used to launch drone and missile attacks.The latest assault also comes as Kyiv seeks to demonstrate that it remains capable of striking deep inside Russia, while Moscow continues to project victory in the war as inevitable. US-mediated negotiations have so far failed to produce a breakthrough.The extent of the damage caused by the latest Ukrainian strikes remained unclear, as Russian federal and local authorities rarely disclose detailed information about the impact of such attacks.
Article Summary: Russia says its air defence systems intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones on Monday. It appeared to be Kyiv’s largest aerial assault since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Ukraine has stepped up its long- range drone attacks on Russian territory.

A massive fire ripped through a commercial building on Thailand's southern resort island of Phuket early on Monday, killing at least 11 people and leaving 16 others injured, police told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the early hours of the morning and quickly spread to several nearby buildings, triggering a major firefighting operation.The fire erupted at around 3.17am local time (2017 GMT) at a shophouse housing a vehicle rental business. Firefighters battled the flames for nearly two hours before bringing the blaze under control, Thai authorities said.Of the 16 injured, 15 were Thai nationals while one was from Myanmar, police said. No tourists were among those killed or injured in the incident.The building is located in a town area near Patong, one of Phuket's most popular beach destinations on the island's western coast. The incident raised concerns as the fire spread beyond the building where it first broke out, engulfing several neighbouring structures.The cause of the fire remains under investigation, with authorities yet to establish what triggered the blaze.The incident comes just four months after a deadly fire at a bar in Bangkok claimed at least 27 lives, highlighting another major fire tragedy in Thailand.Make the intro more directRemove repeated fire detailsUse a sharper news structure

Article Title: 'Perfectly safe' but not 'maxed out'? Trump takes Qatar-gifted jet to Asia
Article Text:
60-day makeover done? Trump takes Qatar's jet to Asia as questions linger

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump is set to fly to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar, but questions remain over whether the plane has undergone the extensive security upgrades that the White House had planned for MAGA supremo, NBC News reported, citing two US officials.The aircraft's planned overhaul had drawn attention in July after a security threat from Iran forced Trump to fly back from Turkey aboard a secret military plane. The incident raised questions about the security arrangements surrounding the Qatari-gifted jet.Trump is expected to visit the Philippines to attend the Asean Summit, a key gathering of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), the regional bloc's highest decision-making forum.Trump had repeatedly said the aircraft would be taken out of service for major modifications so it could “go into any territory”. In September, he said the work would “take about 60 days”. However, the aircraft continued to be used for presidential travel, including a trip to Ireland that month and several journeys during Trump's October midterm campaign blitz.According to NBC News, the plane has undergone periodic maintenance and received some improvements, but it is unclear whether the larger security upgrades have been completed.One of the officials said a longer period of upgrades was still expected, although the work would not take the full 60 days.The changes made so far have reportedly focused largely on the aircraft's interior. One official described them as “cosmetic” enhancements, which did not include the more extensive work the White House had earlier said was planned.A senior administration official declined to discuss the specific modifications, telling NBC News: “We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once. We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.Trump had first spoken about the planned overhaul in July, saying the aircraft already had considerable capabilities but would soon be sent for further modifications.“But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.”He did not explain what the proposed upgrades would involve. The White House has also not clarified why the initial estimate of around 30 days later increased to 60 days.Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had said in July that the aircraft was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel. However, she confirmed that further work was planned, saying it would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump is set to fly to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar. But questions remain over whether the plane has undergone the extensive security upgrades that the White House had planned for Trump. The aircraft's planned overhaul had drawn attention in July after a security threat from Iran forced Trump to fly back from Turkey aboard a secret military plane. The incident raised questions about the security arrangements surrounding the Qatari-gifted jet.

A fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season.Videos shared on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising near the stadium in East Rutherford and drifting over the playing field. One video also captured flames and black smoke erupting from the area near the venue.New Jersey State Police said troopers responded to a report of smoke shortly after 5:50 pm near Lot A and the stadium's American Express gate. They found a fire in an empty postgame tent, according to a report by Fox 5 New York.Fire crews brought the second-alarm blaze under control. No injuries or further damage were reported, while the cause of the fire was not immediately known.ESPN reporter Rich Cimini posted on social media that an announcement had been made inside the stadium about a “structure fire” near the adjacent train station. He later advised people to stay away from the stadium's east plaza, on the train station side, as smoke spread across the venue.Around 20 minutes later, he posted that the “situation has been resolved”.An NJ Transit spokesperson, quoted by NY Post said the fire did not disrupt train services in the area.The blaze broke out hours after the Jets lost 31-12 to the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium. The defeat marked their fifth straight loss, leaving them with a 2-8 record for the season.The Jets struggled against the Bills, who secured a 19-point victory. The loss extended New York's losing streak and added to a difficult season for the team.
Article Summary: Fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday. The blaze sent thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season. No injuries or further damage were reported. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Article Title: US govt seeks 24-year jail, Nikhil Gupta pleads for 12
Article Text:
Indian national Nikhil Gupta pens emotional letter to US district judge

US State Department is learnt to have asked for 24 years in jail for Nikhil Gupta, the Indian national facing trial for an alleged assassination attempt on designated terrorist and chief of Sikhs For Justice group Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.Gupta's counsel have requested a reduced sentence of 12 years while submitting a remorse letter to the judge ahead of sentencing Nov 20. They have requested the judge to consider the probation department's recommendation of a similar-duration jail term besides Gupta pleading guilty and not wasting the court's time. Prosecutors have, however, asked to consider his act of planning a murder on foreign soil as brazen and asked for the maximum sentence.Nikhil Gupta has claimed to be a victim of deception and claimed that he was promised by an individual to settle cases in exchange for plotting the killing.In Feb, Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit it, and money laundering conspiracy which carry a statutory jail term of around 40 years. With this, he may be looking at a reduced sentence through an "acceptance of responsibility" credit.Gupta (54), sources said, may receive a two- to three-level reduction, the standard reward for saving the court the time and expense of a trial. "But if US prosecutors prevail, a 20-year sentence seems likely. Gupta may have to serve around 80% of the awarded jail time with all parameters like good behaviour etc in place," said a source.Under the United States law, if he receives a sentence longer than 12 months, he would be eligible for up to a 15% reduction (roughly two months a year) for good behaviour while incarcerated. Gupta has been held at the Brooklyn detention centre since his 2024 extradition from Prague.
Article Summary: Gupta has been held at the Brooklyn detention centre since his 2024 extradition from Prague. His counsel have requested a reduced sentence of 12 years while submitting a remorse letter to the judge ahead of sentencing Nov 20. If he gets more than 12 months, Gupta may be eligible for term reduction of up to 15%

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: Trump calls Newsom's decision to change 548 death sentences ‘disaster for justice in America’
Article Text:

US President Donald Trump has criticised California Governor Gavin Newsom for commuting the death sentences of 548 inmates, calling the decision a setback for the country's justice system and urging authorities to reverse it.In his first public response to Newsom's decision, Trump took to Truth Social on Saturday to question the governor's handling of the cases, arguing that the move had disregarded the severity of the crimes and the suffering of victims' families."Many of these names, people who have killed, over and over again, can't believe their luck in having a Governor so incompetent and insensitive that he would not let the long and winding legal system prevail," Trump wrote.He described the mass commutations as "a disaster for Justice in America" and said families of murder victims had been left devastated by the decision."Hopefully this decision will be overturned!" the president added, referring to the governor's action. Trump also described the inmates as among the most dangerous murderers in the country's history.Newsom announced the commutations as part of his opposition to capital punishment, maintaining that executions conflict with California's values and undermine the state's legal system.The governor acknowledged that his decision would cause further distress to relatives of victims but said he considered it the right course of action.The move has also drawn objections from victims' families. Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped and murdered in 1993, criticised the governor's decision. Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in 1996.Klaas told the California Post that the commutation decision brought his daughter's killer closer to the possibility of release, describing the move as deeply offensive to families whose relatives were murdered.The decision is also facing potential legal challenges. Anne Marie Schubert, a former district attorney who heads the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, told the New York Post that her organisation intended to challenge the commutations in court. She questioned whether the governor had reviewed each case individually, taking into account the circumstances of the crimes and their impact on victims' families.Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer has also asked the California Supreme Court to block the commutations. Under state law, clemency for individuals convicted of multiple felonies requires approval from the state's highest court before taking effect.California has not carried out an execution since 2006. Newsom introduced a moratorium on executions in 2019, although the state continues to hold the country's largest death row population.The decision could also bring additional scrutiny to Newsom as he considers a possible presidential campaign in 2028.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump criticises California Governor Gavin Newsom for commuting the death sentences of 548 inmates. Newsom announced the commutations as part of his opposition to capital punishment, maintaining that executions conflict with California's values and undermine the state's legal system. The move has also drawn objections from victims' families.

Article Title: UN chief hopes Donald Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will lead to nuclear disarmament efforts
Article Text:

China calls trilateral meeting significant for global stability

The United Nations is ready to support any efforts towards nuclear disarmament that emerge from this week's meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Monday, while cautioning that such an outcome was not guaranteed.Speaking at a press conference in Manila, where he is attending a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Guterres said the UN would be willing to contribute to any denuclearisation programme agreed upon by the three countries.“If there is a denuclearisation program, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success,” he said.“This is what we would like to see. It's not yet guaranteed that we will get there,” he added.US President Donald Trump is expected to raise nuclear arms reduction efforts during his November 19 meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The White House said last week that the issue would be on the agenda.The three leaders are scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, southern China.China's Foreign Ministry described the proposed meeting as being of “groundbreaking significance”, saying it could promote world peace and stability, Reuters reported.Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday that it would be the first face-to-face meeting between the heads of state of China, Russia and the United States.“They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” Mao told reporters in Beijing.She said the three countries had an important responsibility to work together to address global challenges and promote stability.“Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries,” she added.Mao said closer communication would also meet the expectations of the international community and help stabilise the global situation and advance dialogue and cooperation. She did not disclose specific details of the meeting's agenda.Trump's push to make nuclear arms reductions a focus of the talks has drawn objections from Beijing, which has resisted direct negotiations with Washington over its nuclear programme. China has argued that the United States and Russia should discuss the issue directly because of their much larger nuclear arsenals.Guterres also reiterated the UN's call for a diplomatic process to end the US-Israeli war against Iran, another issue Trump is expected to raise at the summit.“What we need in relation to the situation in the Middle East, and in particular in relation to Iran and the United States, is a serious diplomatic process of negotiation to end this neither peace nor war that you are living in with devastating consequences to the global economy,” the UN chief said.The UN has repeatedly advocated nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tensions and competition among major powers have increased global nuclear risks.Trump's four-day Asia trip also includes a visit to the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is due to meet Asean leaders and attend the first meeting of the Quad grouping of the United States, India, Australia and Japan in two years.
Article Summary: The United Nations is ready to support any efforts towards nuclear disarmament that emerge from this week's meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia. US President Donald Trump is expected to raise nuclear arms reduction efforts during his November 19 meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

When Pearl Oguchi entered a technology workplace, finding someone who shared her experience as a Black woman was often difficult. After years of navigating an industry where she rarely encountered other women engineers or Black colleagues, she decided to create the support network she wished she had. What began as a Facebook group has since grown into Black Women in Tech, a global community of more than 50,000 members who exchange job referrals, review CVs, share professional advice and support one another through workplace challenges.Oguchi, who has spent 22 years working in technology, was recently recognised for her contribution to the industry. She received the Lifetime Impact in STEM award at the 2026 Overt STEM Awards, held at Unity Place in Milton Keynes on November 3. According to Business MK, the recognition acknowledged her career in technology and her work founding the Black Women in Tech community.Her journey towards building the network was shaped by her own professional experiences. A July 2026 profile in Build Your Power Careers Magazine, titled 'Building Your Own Table: How Grassroots Communities Are Saving Careers and Lives', described how Oguchi encountered isolation while working in software engineering.When she joined Meta's UK office in 2016, she was reportedly the first quality assurance (QA) professional hired there. Across her years in software engineering, she had encountered only two female engineers and no other Black women in the field. The lack of people with similar experiences made it difficult to find the kind of professional connections and understanding that could help her navigate her career.Rather than wait for an organisation to create such a space, Oguchi decided to build one herself. Drawing on Meta's culture of taking initiative and solving problems, she started a Facebook group called Black Women in Tech. The idea was to create a place where women could connect with others facing similar experiences, exchange knowledge and find opportunities that might otherwise remain difficult to access.The group grew organically, eventually crossing the 50,000-member mark. Its members use the platform to share job opportunities and referrals, review one another's CVs, exchange resources and discuss their experiences in corporate workplaces. The community also offers a space for women to seek advice from people who understand the particular challenges of building careers in technology.The network has even helped some members make significant career transitions, including women moving from fast-food jobs into technology roles with the support and guidance available through the group. Its purpose extends beyond professional networking, creating connections that can help members build confidence and explore new career possibilities.Alongside her community-building work, Oguchi has developed a career spanning engineering, product management and technology delivery. She spent nine years at Meta, working on products and systems used at different scales, from specialised platforms serving thousands of people to global products reaching billions. She is also the founder of Qube Catalyst, through which she works with technology companies and startups on product development and growth.The Overt STEM Awards recognised several individuals and organisations working to improve access to science, technology, engineering and mathematics careers across the Oxford-Cambridge Growth Corridor. More than 50 finalists attended the November 3 ceremony. Other winners included Natalie Desty, founder of STEM Returners, who received the Women in STEM Champion award, and STEM On Track, which was named the overall STEM Champion.For Oguchi, the community she created has grown far beyond the original purpose of finding professional connections. It has become a network where women can exchange opportunities, learn from one another and find support from people who understand their experiences. Her initiative demonstrates how an individual response to workplace isolation can develop into a professional community connecting tens of thousands of people.
Article Summary: Pearl Oguchi started a Facebook group called Black Women in Tech. The group grew organically, eventually crossing the 50,000-member mark. Members exchange job referrals, review CVs, share professional advice and support one another through workplace challenges. Oguchi was recently recognised for her contribution to the technology industry.

Article Title: A New York couple with three children say a downstairs neighbour screamed threats and repeatedly called police; a judge issued a temporary order as their landlord sought at least $550,000 in a lawsuit

A dispute between neighbours in a Manhattan apartment building has led to a lawsuit seeking at least $550,000 in damages and legal fees. According to a New York Post report, the building's owner has accused a 72-year-old tenant of repeatedly disturbing families living in the apartment above hers. The allegations include verbal abuse, threats, prolonged banging on the ceiling and repeated police complaints.The latest family to report problems is that of Tara and Riad Abrahams, who moved into the four-bedroom apartment with their three children in November 2025. They have alleged that their neighbour, Anne Stockton, made their children feel unsafe at home. Their complaints also describe incidents in which police were called over alleged noise during ordinary family activities.The building owner, which operates the property at 85 East End Avenue on Manhattan's Upper East Side, claims that the complaints are part of a pattern extending over several years. According to its lawsuit, three families who previously occupied the same apartment also experienced similar problems and eventually moved out.The case has now resulted in a temporary restraining order. A Manhattan judge signed the order days after the landlord filed its complaint.It prohibits Stockton from making unreasonable noise or engaging in conduct described as assaulting, menacing, intimidating or threatening towards the tenants and children living upstairs.The lawsuit also raises a separate financial dispute. The landlord claims Stockton has accumulated nearly $88,000 in unpaid rent. She disputes the amount, according to the ongoing litigation.The Abrahams family said the problems began after they took possession of their apartment. According to the court documents, Stockton repeatedly shouted at them and used abusive language.The family also accused her of striking the ceiling with an object that sounded like a lead pipe. They claimed the banging sometimes continued for hours.Another concern was the number of police calls. The landlord's complaint alleges that Stockton contacted the police at least 10 times, making accusations that the building owner described as unsupported.The family said the incidents were not limited to particular times of the day. Their complaints included occasions when their teenage daughter was alone at home, eating lunch or completing schoolwork.For the parents, the effect on their children became a major concern. Tara Abrahams told the court that the neighbour's outbursts could be heard by the children and alleged that this was intentional.Her husband described how their 10-year-old son had begun questioning the family about the situation. "My 10-year-old son now constantly asks me, ‘What did we do wrong? Why does the lady on the 10th floor hate us?’" Riad Abrahams wrote in a sworn affidavit. "I do not know how to answer him," he added.He said the children had become frightened inside their own home and were reluctant to remain in the apartment without their parents.One incident mentioned in the family's complaints involved their eldest daughter's 16th birthday. The family had gathered for dinner and was opening presents when Stockton allegedly contacted the police. Tara Abrahams described the incident in an email to the landlord, which was included in the court filing.Riad also wrote about the episode, alleging that the neighbour shouted at the family and repeatedly referred to them as "animals".The landlord's complaint says several of Stockton's noise allegations were investigated by building staff without the reported disturbance being established.A worker cited in the court papers described what happened when the building manager questioned Stockton about the source of the noise. She reportedly claimed that the sound was coming from her own kitchen cabinet.The family approached the landlord with complaints about the repeated confrontations and their impact on the children. The dispute eventually became part of the legal action against Stockton.The landlord's case also relies on complaints from people who occupied the apartment before the Abrahams family. It alleges that the problems began at least in 2013.Jennifer Gaydos Stephan was among the earlier residents. She lived in the apartment with her then-husband, Scott Hartman, and their four children.Speaking to The New York Post, Stephan said Stockton frequently struck the ceiling with a broom and left unpleasant messages outside their apartment. The notes allegedly asked the parents to control their children's noise. "She was a disaster," Stephan said.Stephan said she enjoyed living in the building but eventually decided to leave. Her family moved out after about two years because they could no longer tolerate the situation.A 2014 email from her then-husband to the landlord also appears in the lawsuit. He alleged that Stockton had threatened to discipline their children herself. The message described another incident in which she allegedly confronted two of the children inside an elevator. The family said they were unwilling to continue living in conditions they considered unsafe.Mitch Jacaruso, who occupied the apartment from 2014, also reported problems. In a 2017 email to the landlord, he alleged that Stockton had shouted at his children, then aged 11 and eight, inside the building's elevator.According to his complaint, she called them "animals and horrible children" and threatened legal action against them. The landlord's lawsuit says the incident eventually led Jacaruso to leave the building.The following tenant, Mark Weiss, reported similar concerns despite his children visiting the apartment only occasionally.In one message to the landlord, Weiss said his daughter was frightened and did not want to leave the apartment. In another email from 2019, he complained that the repeated banging on the ceiling was upsetting his children.He also reported that Stockton had come to his apartment again and said the situation was becoming a serious concern. Weiss remained in the apartment until 2024. The Abrahams family moved in approximately a year after his departure.The building owner's complaint includes allegations about Stockton's rent payments. A ledger cited in the court papers reportedly shows that she began paying rent irregularly in 2018.The landlord claims there were no major payments after 2022, apart from $24,000 received through the state's Emergency Rental Assistance Program last spring. Even after that assistance, the alleged outstanding amount stands at nearly $88,000. Stockton disputes the arrears, and the matter remains part of the ongoing litigation.She has lived in the building since 1992 and occupies a rent-stabilised apartment on the 10th floor. Her monthly rent is $1,775, according to the lawsuit.The landlord is seeking at least $550,000 in damages and legal expenses. The temporary court order separately restricts Stockton's conduct towards the family living above her.

A Manhattan judge signed the order days after the landlord filed its complaint. A temporary restraining order prohibits Anne Stockton from making unreasonable noise or engaging in conduct described as assaulting, menacing, intimidating or threatening towards the tenants and children.

Article Title: A handwritten 1902 deed split mineral rights beneath 117.55 acres in West Virginia; 124 years later, the state's top court ruled descendants held only one-sixteenth of the oil and gas, not the one-hal
Article Text:
Image credits: Canva AI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A handwritten property deed from 1902 has become the centre of a century-old ownership dispute in the US, with a court ruling that a family's claim to half the oil and gas beneath a piece of land was worth only one-sixteenth. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia delivered its decision on November 12, 2026, upholding an earlier appellate ruling that interpreted the original document according to its exact wording. The dispute concerned mineral rights beneath 117.55 acres in Doddridge County, West Virginia, and involved the successors of two families connected to the land more than 120 years ago.The case, titled 'Severin POA Group, LLC v. Nicholson', centred on a deed written by F.W. Severin on April 1, 1902. At the time, Severin owned the surface, oil, gas and mineral rights across a 224-acre property in Doddridge County. He subsequently transferred 117.55 acres to L.D. Nicholson while retaining a portion of the mineral rights for himself. The crucial detail was a handwritten reservation in the deed. Severin retained "the one sixteenth of all the oil and gas in and under said land". More than a century later, the meaning of those words became the subject of a legal battle after oil and gas production began beneath the property.The dispute emerged after the property's oil and gas rights were leased to Rockwell Petroleum Company in 1977. The lease was subsequently assigned to Antero Resources Corporation. In 1999, Nicholson's successors transferred the property to Earl J. Nicholson and Joyce A. Nicholson. When Antero began producing and selling some of the oil and gas beneath the land in 2017, it started making monthly royalty payments to the Nicholsons.However, disagreements arose over how the royalties should be divided between the Nicholson family and the successors of Severin. The central question was whether the 1902 deed gave Severin's successors one-sixteenth of the entire mineral estate or whether that fraction represented half of the oil and gas ownership.The Circuit Court of Doddridge County ruled in September 2022 in favour of the Severin successors, represented by Severin POA Group, LLC. It concluded that the one-sixteenth reservation effectively represented a one-half interest in the mineral estate, taking into account historical practices in the oil and gas industry.The Nicholsons challenged that interpretation, arguing that the wording was straightforward and that one-sixteenth meant exactly what it said. In November 2023, the Intermediate Court of Appeals of West Virginia overturned the lower court's decision, holding that Severin had reserved only one-sixteenth of the oil and gas beneath the property. The dispute subsequently reached the state's highest court, which agreed with the appellate court.In its November 12 opinion, the Supreme Court of Appeals said the deed was unambiguous and that the language had to be interpreted according to its ordinary meaning. The judges rejected the argument that industry conventions in the early 1900s could transform the stated one-sixteenth interest into a one-half share.Severin successors had argued that one-eighth was historically treated as a reference to the entire mineral estate in certain oil and gas transactions. They claimed that Severin intended to retain half of that supposed one-eighth interest, which would explain the one-sixteenth figure written in the deed. The court, however, distinguished between ownership of mineral rights and royalty payments received under oil and gas leases. It noted that one-eighth was commonly used as a royalty rate in historical leases, but that did not mean it represented ownership of the entire mineral estate.Judges also rejected a legal principle known as the "estate misconception theory", which has been adopted in Texas. Under that approach, certain old mineral-rights documents using one-eighth fractions can be presumed to refer to the entire mineral estate.West Virginia's highest court declined to introduce a similar presumption, saying it could create confusion and undermine the stability of property titles.The court concluded that Severin had reserved one-sixteenth of the oil and gas beneath the property, exactly as the deed stated. It therefore affirmed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' decision. Justice Flanigan delivered the opinion, while Justice Kirkpatrick dissented and reserved the right to write separately.
Article Summary: A handwritten property deed from 1902 has become the centre of a century-old ownership dispute in the US. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia delivered its decision on November 12, 2026, upholding an earlier appellate ruling. The dispute concerned mineral rights beneath 117.55 acres in Doddridge County, West Virginia, and involved the successors of two families.

Read more about it, as per the reports, here:Chew has always enjoyed the atmosphere of a fair. He liked the Ferris wheel, the animal shows, the food, and the way so many different kinds of entertainment could be found in one place. After retiring, he came across a Facebook page called “Visit All 50 States.” That gave him the idea to do something even more specific, visit all 50 state fairs. “I just thought, I’d do that even better and visit all 50 state fairs,” he told The Washington Post. “It was something different.”Chew began with the Georgia State Fair in October 2023. His second stop, the Florida State Fair in Tampa, remains one of his favourites.Since then, he has visited fairs from Georgia to California, taking in butter sculptures, carnival games, agricultural exhibits, and live entertainment. His most recent stop was the Louisiana State Fair, where he rode a multicolored slide and watched a Wild West show.He has also tried local foods that reflect each region. In Louisiana, he sampled gumbo, crawfish, étouffée, and alligator bites. In Utah, he tried Mexican street corn for the first time.Chew initially thought all state fairs would feel similar. Instead, he found that each one has its own character, shaped by local food, traditions, and community pride. At the Florida State Fair, which is set around a lake, he watched performances from the water’s edge. At the California State Fair, he encountered a “cannabis village,” something he described as “pretty crazy.”He tries to skip vendors that travel from fair to fair, preferring local food and exhibits that give each stop its own flavour. That approach has helped him see the fairs as more than just rides and fried food.Chew travels to the fairs alone, but he says he never feels lonely. “I make friends everywhere I go,” he told The Washington Post. Some of his best moments come from talking with strangers and learning about their lives. He has found that people are often proud of their hometown or home state, and that pride shows in how they talk about their local fair.In Osceola, Iowa, he got off a train in August 2025 and realised there were no rides or taxis available to take him to his hotel. The stationmaster ended up giving him a ride, an example of the kind of kindness he has encountered along the way.Chew uses a colour-coded spreadsheet to track fair dates and locations. He tries to group nearby stops into week-long itineraries, since many fairs happen in August and can be hard to schedule together. He prefers to drive or take the train when possible, flying only when necessary. He also builds in side trips to local sites along the way, using the fair circuit as a way to see more of the country. “It’s a lot of planning,” he said, adding that he spends as much time planning as he does traveling. “I spend as much time planning as I do going.”For Chew, state fairs offer a connection to a version of American life that feels increasingly distant. He sees them as a “real cross section of America” and a way to experience traditions that have lasted for generations.Jon Kay, an associate professor of folklore at Indiana University, told The Washington Post that fairs are more than rides and food. They are a way for people to express community values and bring generations together.For Chew, the appeal is simpler. He loves the sounds, sights, smells, and energy of a fair, and he enjoys seeing kids show animals and compete in various events.Chew expects to visit his final fair in Oregon in summer 2030. Alaska, Nebraska, and Minnesota are among the states still on his list. He is not sure what he will do after that, but he is already thinking about it. “I guess I’ll be looking for something else to do after that,” he told The Washington Post.For now, the mission continues. One fair at a time, Chew is seeing the country, meeting people, and finding purpose in retirement.
Article Summary: Jim Chew, 78, has visited 31 state fairs across the country and has 19 more to go. He expects to visit his final fair in Oregon in 2030. Chew uses retirement savings, careful planning, and a willingness to travel alone.

Article Title: In Maine, more than 28 cyclists carried Thanksgiving turkeys on their bikes rather than in cars; their November 14 delivery helped 58 families receive free holiday meals through a Camden food pantry

More than 28 cyclists in Maine traded cars for bicycles to deliver Thanksgiving turkeys to families in need, turning a routine holiday donation drive into an unusual community event. On November 14, riders gathered in Rockport, collected turkeys and other Thanksgiving essentials from a supermarket and transported the donations on their bikes to a local food pantry in Camden. Their efforts helped 58 families receive a free turkey for their Thanksgiving dinner.According to WABI-TV, the event was the eighth annual Turkey Ride, organised through a partnership between Maine Sport Rockport and the Camden Area Christian Food Pantry. Instead of arranging a conventional vehicle-based collection, organisers invited participants to purchase holiday groceries and carry them to the pantry on bicycles. The event combined cycling with volunteering, giving participants an opportunity to support local families while taking part in a festive outdoor activity.The ride began at Maine Sport Rockport, where participants gathered before setting off along two possible routes to Hannaford Supermarkets.At the supermarket, cyclists picked up frozen turkeys and other Thanksgiving favourites before continuing to the Camden Area Christian Food Pantry to drop off their donations. The sight of cyclists navigating the roads with turkeys strapped to their bikes gave the annual initiative its distinctive character.The donations made a direct difference to households in the area. According to WABI, 58 families received a turkey free of charge for their Thanksgiving dinner. The organisers said the initiative offered riders a way to contribute to something meaningful while bringing attention to the food pantry and its work.Peggy Baum, vice-president of the Camden Area Christian Food Pantry, said the community had consistently supported the organisation over the years. She added that the ride helped participants connect with a cause they considered important. "Our community has supported this pantry enormously over the years," Baum told WABI-TV, describing the event as a colourful and enjoyable way for cyclists to give back.Debra Milliken, president of the food pantry, highlighted the unusual sight of the participants arriving with their donations. Recalling the procession of cyclists, she said: "If you could see them coming up the street, 30 cyclists coming up over that steep hill with turkeys on their backs."The Turkey Ride has now become an annual tradition, with its eighth edition continuing a community effort that brings together local businesses, volunteers and residents. The involvement of Maine Sport Rockport also allowed the event to combine outdoor recreation with a charitable initiative, making it accessible to people interested in both cycling and community service.The Camden Area Christian Food Pantry serves several communities in the region, including Appleton, Camden, Hope, Islesboro, Lincolnville, Rockport, Searsmont, Union and Washington. Its official website says the organisation welcomes anyone in need of assistance.It operates as an all-volunteer, non-profit organisation and relies on contributions from individuals, businesses, civic groups, schools and churches.The pantry also regularly updates its website and social media pages with items that are most urgently needed, encouraging residents to contribute groceries and financial support. Its work extends beyond seasonal events such as the Turkey Ride, helping households manage their weekly food budgets throughout the year.
